title: The Executor inventory carries a single current pointer and a shared ordinal space, so one checkout cannot serve a Metal and a CUDA host and two checkouts can mint the same id

evidence.note: B300 checkout after releasing Executor v92 against the captured CUDA host: inventory/EXECUTOR_REVISIONS.json now names v92 as current with 91 superseded, and host_admitted and profiler_admitted are both true

Apple checkout, unchanged at v91 (metal). Its launch path reads tools/launch_task.py:110-113, which resolves CURRENT_RELEASE_BINDING and then requires the resolved host kind to be metal; adopting v92 as current here would refuse every Metal campaign

the collision this finding described was then caused, one commit after describing it. The server had released v95+e6a9959e; this checkout could not see that descriptor, so its own release cycle minted v95+4314d9a9 over different bytes. Neither was committed and neither had been consumed by campaign evidence, so it was recoverable: the locally minted one was withdrawn, the server's descriptor was imported so the released set was visible, and re-releasing produced v96+4314d9a9 -- the same content digest under the correct ordinal, which is what confirms only the number was wrong

observation: A Study template may bind only CURRENT_RELEASE_BINDING, and lab/bindings.py resolves that to inventory/EXECUTOR_REVISIONS.json's single current entry. A frozen Study instead names one exact Executor by id, path and digest. Both are right for one execution host, which is what the Lab had. With an Apple M2 and an NVIDIA B300 in use at once there is no value of current that serves both: the Apple launcher refuses a host whose kind is not metal, and a CUDA campaign needs the CUDA host to be current. The file is tracked, so the two checkouts diverge permanently in a version-controlled artifact, and every sync has to reconcile a pointer by hand. This is a property of the model rather than a defect in either host: nothing is silently wrong today, and both checkouts are internally consistent. Bringing the CUDA host up surfaced a second and sharper face of the same model, which the first reading of this finding missed. The release cycle derives the next Executor ordinal from the largest one it can see released *in its own checkout*, so two checkouts that have not been synchronised will both mint the same number over different bytes. This nearly happened: the B300 checkout stood at v92 while the Apple checkout had already released v93, so a release on the server would have produced a second v93. That is not a divergence a later merge can reconcile, because AGENTS.md holds that a released descriptor reserves its identity and is never reused or deleted -- two different v93 bytes would leave the ledger permanently ambiguous about which one any evidence refers to. It was avoided by releasing on the Apple side first and synchronising the server before its own release, which is a procedure rather than a property: nothing in the tooling enforces the ordering. The procedure is not sufficient, and the proof is that it failed immediately. Having just written that releasing on two hosts requires synchronising them in a fixed order, the very next release on the Apple side minted a second v95 -- because synchronising had been done in one direction only. The server had been brought up to date from this checkout, but the descriptor the server then released was never brought back, so the release cycle here still believed the released set topped out at v94. Nothing warned. The cycle reports the id it is about to mint and proceeds, because from inside one checkout a gap in the sequence and an unsynchronised peer are indistinguishable. It was caught only because the ordinal was being watched deliberately; a release run without that attention would have committed the duplicate and the ledger would then have carried two different byte sequences under one reserved identity, which is the state the reservation rule exists to prevent and which no later merge can resolve. Building the guard turned up that the behaviour was not merely unguarded but asserted. tests/contracts/test_executor.py held a fixture with two worktrees that released against the same history, and it required both to produce a v47 and required the two to differ -- the collision, written down as the contract. It also required a duplicate raised *within* one checkout to be refused, so the codebase distinguished duplicates it could see from duplicates it could not and accepted the second kind.
proposed_change: Resolve the Executor by what the requested backend needs rather than by a single global pointer -- the route a backend declares already implies its host kind, so a template binding could name a route and the inventory could carry one current per host kind. That changes the Study template contract in lab/bindings.py and needs the frozen-Study semantics thought through, so it is deliberately not being done alongside a campaign bring-up. Recorded now so the interim does not become permanent by omission. The ordinal space needs the same treatment as the pointer. Deriving the next id from what a single checkout happens to see makes correctness depend on an operator remembering to sync first; the release cycle should either refuse when it cannot prove it has seen every released descriptor, or take the identity from something that does not depend on local visibility. Until then, releasing on two hosts requires synchronising the checkouts in a fixed order and that requirement should be written where a release is run, not inferred. Reclassified from capacity to bug on that evidence: this is not a limit that inconveniences a two-host setup, it is a way to corrupt the identity ledger silently while following the documented procedure. The minimum is that the release cycle must refuse to mint when it cannot establish it has seen every released descriptor, rather than inferring the next ordinal from local visibility alone. What the guard now closes and what it does not are worth separating, because closing part of it is not closing it. A checkout will not mint while holding a descriptor it has not published, will not mint while its remote carries descriptors it lacks, and will not mint when it cannot check unless the operator states why -- and verifying an unchanged release is deliberately not gated, since it mints nothing. What remains open is the window between one host releasing and publishing: nothing can see another working tree's untracked files, so a peer with an up-to-date remote can still mint the same ordinal during it. That window is what actually caught this project out, and it is narrowed rather than removed -- the host that opens it can no longer mint again until it closes it. Removing it needs an identity that does not depend on local visibility, or a ledger both hosts can reach; the B300 has no egress, so it releases under the isolated acknowledgement and its releases are exactly the ones the remote check cannot cover. The test now asserts both halves so neither is mistaken for the other.
verification_plan: Capacity finding, verified by construction rather than by campaign: one checkout resolves a Metal Executor for a Metal backend and a CUDA Executor for a Triton backend in the same working tree, with no hand edit of the inventory between them, and both hosts' campaigns start.
